title: Light That Bounces Again
description: Umbra hides the shard in a dark vault with a single window. Arjun bounces a beam off mirror after mirror to reach it — proving reflected light can be reflected again.

content.value: A ray of light that has already been reflected can hit another mirror and reflect a second time — and a third, and a fourth. Each bounce still obeys the laws of reflection. This is how light can be 'steered' around corners.

☀️ ─▶ 🪞 ─▶ 🪞 ─▶ 👁️
light bounces off mirror 1, then mirror 2, into the eye

Because we can bounce light again and again, we can send it exactly where we want. Two mirrors set at the right angles can carry light up and over a wall — this is the idea behind a PERISCOPE used in submarines to see above the water.

Multiple reflection is used in dentists' mirrors (to see behind teeth), in kaleidoscopes (to multiply patterns), and in fibre-optic cables that carry internet signals as bouncing light. Repeated reflection is everywhere!
Every bounce loses a little light, so after many reflections the image gets dimmer. That is why a very long mirror tunnel fades into darkness.
Key Takeaway: Light that has been reflected can be reflected again and again, each time obeying the laws of reflection — letting us steer light around corners.

quiz.question: Can a ray of light that has already reflected off one mirror reflect off a second mirror?
options: No, light can only reflect once
Yes, and it still obeys the laws of reflection each time
Only if the mirrors are coloured
quiz.explain: Reflected light can be reflected again and again. Every bounce obeys i = r.

quiz.question: A submarine periscope lets sailors see above the water using…
options: two mirrors that reflect light twice around a bend
quiz.explain: A periscope uses two mirrors so light reflects twice, carrying the view from above down to the viewer's eye.

quiz.question: After many reflections, an image usually becomes…
options: dimmer, because a little light is lost each bounce
quiz.explain: Each reflection loses a little light, so repeated bounces make the image gradually dimmer.
